  Checks to run on the tables before you rely on them: dates, months, keys,
  length of stay, code shapes and empty values.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
# Print results at most 60 characters wide, "#> " included, to fit a printed page.
options(width = 57)
# Keep the build machine out of printed query headers (load duckdb first, as it
# registers its own description when it loads).
loadNamespace("duckdb")
registerS3method("db_connection_describe", "duckdb_connection",
                 function(con, ...) "example database", envir = asNamespace("dbplyr"))
```

The [Worked example](getting-started.html) trusted its tables; on THIP, run
these checks before you do. Your code rests on assumptions about the data: that
dates can be read, that each record appears once, that codes are written the
way your comparisons expect. When one fails, the code does not stop: a filter
on a date that could not be read drops the record, and a comparison with
`"K35"` misses `"k358"`, without a message. A check turns silent failures like
these into counts you can see.

Each section below says what one check tests, gives the code, and says what to
look for and what to do about it. The code brings back only summaries: counts,
never records.

The example database is invented, with a few values damaged on purpose ([Meet
the THIP data](meet-the-data.html)), so its results show how each check works,
not what THIP's tables hold. On THIP, connect with `thip_connect()` instead and
run every check on the tables you use.

## The tables to check

Stack the tables you will use, with their dates converted. This is the
`admissions` query from [From question to cohort](question-to-cohort.html):

```{r admissions}
library(thipR)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

con <- thip_connect_example()

admissions <- thip_table(
  con,
  tables = c("nhso2565", "nhso2566", "nhso2567"),
  .id = "source_table",
  dates = c(adm = "dateadm", dsc = "datedsc"),
  date_format = c(adm = "%Y%m%d", dsc = "%Y%m%d")
)
```

## Dates that cannot be read

`thip_date_audit()` compares each converted date with its raw text and counts,
for each table, the values that were missing, blank, parsed (read) or failed;
[From question to
cohort](question-to-cohort.html#audit-the-dates-before-you-filter) explains
each count. Audit both dates, table by table:

```{r date-audit}
date_audit <- thip_date_audit(
  admissions,
  columns = c(adm = "dateadm", dsc = "datedsc"),
  by = "source_table"
)

date_audit |>
  arrange(field, source_table) |>
  select(-raw_column) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Every admission date was read. Of the discharge dates,
`r sum(date_audit$n_failed)` failed and `r sum(date_audit$n_blank)` is blank.
To see what the failures say, count the raw text of every discharge date that
did not become a date:

```{r date-failures}
admissions |>
  filter(is.na(dsc)) |>
  count(source_table, datedsc) |>
  arrange(source_table, datedsc)
```

The two failures read `20230229`, 29 February 2023, a day that did not exist.
A date that was read can still be wrong. Count the stays that end before they
start:

```{r date-order}
admissions |>
  filter(dsc < adm) |>
  count(name = "ends_before_start")
```

There are none in the example; the check of `los`, below, compares the dates
further. On your tables, **look for** failed or blank values in any date you
will use, `n_inconsistent` above zero, failures that gather in one table, and
stays that end before they start. Audit every other date you use the same way,
such as `death_date`, whose format is `"%Y-%m-%d"`; most death dates are blank,
which is not a failure.

**What to do.** thipR does not repair dates; you decide what a failure means for
your study. If a step needs the date, as follow-up needs the discharge date, a
record without it cannot take that step: leave it out and count it in your flow
chart. Many failures in one table or one month point to a problem in the data
rather than in single records; raise it with the THIP team.

## Records per month and table

Your study period should sit in months that the tables cover evenly: no month
missing, no sudden jump, and no month held by two tables. Count the records by
table and month of admission, taking the month from the raw text so that every
record counts, even one whose date failed to convert:

```{r monthly}
monthly <- admissions |>
  count(source_table, month = substr(dateadm, 1, 6),
        name = "records") |>
  collect()

monthly |>
  group_by(source_table) |>
  summarise(first = min(month), last = max(month),
            months = n(), fewest = min(records),
            most = max(records))
```

In the example, each table holds the 12 months of its fiscal year, October to
September, so the tables meet with no gap and no shared month. Every month has
between `r min(monthly$records)` and `r max(monthly$records)` records. To see
the months in order, plot one dot per table and month:

```{r monthly-plot, fig.asp = 0.55, fig.alt = "Records per month of admission in the example, October 2021 to September 2024: one dot a month, in an even band with no gaps, jumps or doubled months."}
monthly <- monthly |>
  mutate(first_day = as.Date(paste0(month, "01"),
                             format = "%Y%m%d"))

plot(records ~ first_day, data = monthly,
     ylim = c(0, max(monthly$records)),
     xlab = "Month of admission", ylab = "Records")
```

In the example the dots form an even band. On your tables, **look for** a table
with fewer months than its span from first to last (a gap), two tables with
records in the same month (an overlap: two dots in one month), and a month far
above or below its neighbours (a jump).

**What to do.** Find out why before you study the months involved. Keep the
study period, and the look-back and follow-up windows around it, inside months
the tables cover fully ([Look back and follow
up](look-back-follow-up.html#windows-and-the-years-you-stacked)). Where two
tables share months, check the keys, next, before you count anything in them.

## Each record once

Stacking keeps every row, so a record held by two tables, or twice by one,
counts twice. Count the `tran_id` values that appear more than once, and the
person-days (one person, one admission date) with more than one record:

```{r keys}
admissions |>
  count(tran_id) |>
  filter(n > 1) |>
  count(name = "repeated_ids")

admissions |>
  count(pid, dateadm) |>
  filter(n > 1) |>
  count(name = "repeated_person_days")
```

Both are zero in the example; on your tables, **look for** any count above zero.
The first finds a record that appears twice. Only the second can find one stay
written as two records with different keys.

**What to do.** Look at the records involved side by side, inside THIP: their
tables, dates, diagnoses and discharge status. Two records of one person on one
day may be the same stay twice, a transfer between hospitals, or two real
admissions. Decide how to count each kind, write the rule into your protocol and
count the records it removes. Do not drop repeats with `distinct()` before you
have looked.

## Length of stay against the dates

Some columns record what you could also work out from others. `los`, the length
of stay in days, should follow from the admission and discharge dates. Count the
differences between `los` and the days from admission to discharge; a single
value means the two agree, and shows how `los` counts days:

```{r los}
los_check <- admissions |>
  mutate(days = as.integer(dsc - adm),
         difference = as.integer(los) - days) |>
  count(source_table, difference) |>
  collect() |>
  arrange(source_table, difference)

los_check
```

Wherever both dates were read, `los` is the number of days between them plus 1:
the example counts both the admission day and the discharge day. The
`r sum(los_check$n[is.na(los_check$difference)])` missing differences are the
records whose discharge date failed or is blank. On your tables, **look for**
more than one difference, or differences that gather in one table.

On THIP, `as.integer()` stops the whole query at text that is not a number, such
as an empty `los`. If that happens, count the empty values first, as below, and
see [Working with a database from
R](database-from-r.html#the-example-is-duckdb-thip-is-clickhouse).

**What to do.** Choose which value your study uses, and say why. Windows in this
course are measured from dates, so the dates decide and `los` checks them. Where
the two agree everywhere else, `los` could fill a failed discharge date, as
`adm + los - 1` where, as in the example, `los` counts both days; that is a rule
for your protocol, not a repair to make quietly. Where they disagree, look at
examples before you choose: either column can be the wrong one.

## The shape of codes

THIP's data dictionary describes the diagnosis columns as ICD-10 codes ([Meet
the THIP data](meet-the-data.html#diagnoses-and-procedures)); to check how
yours are written, first count every code in `pdx` and the 20 secondary
diagnosis columns:

```{r codes}
dx_cols <- c("pdx", paste0("sdx", 1:20))

count_codes <- function(column) {
  admissions |>
    count(code = .data[[column]]) |>
    collect() |>
    mutate(column = column)
}

codes <- bind_rows(lapply(dx_cols, count_codes))
```

`count_codes()` counts the values of one column on the database
(`.data[[column]]` is the column whose name is in `column`), and `lapply()` runs
it for each of the `r length(dx_cols)` columns. Only codes and their counts come
into R, so any R function can check their shape. Mark each code's length and
whether it holds lower-case letters or a dot, then count the shapes (`wt = n`
adds up how often each code was written) and list the odd codes:

```{r code-shapes}
shapes <- codes |>
  filter(code != "") |>
  mutate(length = nchar(code),
         lower_case = grepl("[a-z]", code),
         dot = grepl(".", code, fixed = TRUE))

count(shapes, length, lower_case, dot, wt = n)

filter(shapes, lower_case | dot)
```

In the example, codes have three to five characters, and two are odd: `k358`, a
principal diagnosis in lower case, and `E11.9`, a secondary diagnosis with a
dot. On your tables, **look for** lengths you did not expect, lower-case
letters, dots, and spaces, which add to the length.

**What to do.** `thip_filter_icd()` and `icd_flag()` clean codes before they
compare them ([Flag conditions](condition-flags.html#codes-are-cleaned-first));
before your own comparisons, clean them the same way, as in
`toupper(gsub(".", "", trimws(code), fixed = TRUE))`.

## Empty values and ages

`is.na()` finds missing values, `NA`, but not empty text, `""`, so your filters
need to know which one a column holds. Count both in the columns you rely on,
with the same pattern as `count_codes()`:

```{r empty}
key_cols <- c("pid", "tran_id", "sex", "age_y", "dateadm",
              "datedsc", "los", "pdx")

count_empty <- function(column) {
  admissions |>
    summarise(
      missing = sum(is.na(.data[[column]]), na.rm = TRUE),
      blank = sum(.data[[column]] == "", na.rm = TRUE)
    ) |>
    collect() |>
    mutate(column = column, .before = missing)
}

bind_rows(lapply(key_cols, count_empty))
```

No value is `NA`, and the only empty one is the blank discharge date that the
audit found.

Numbers stored as text need a range check. Count the values of `age_y` on the
database, then convert them in R, where text that is not a number becomes `NA`
instead of stopping the query:

```{r ages}
ages <- admissions |>
  count(age_y) |>
  collect() |>
  mutate(age = as.integer(age_y))

range(ages$age, na.rm = TRUE)

ages |>
  filter(is.na(age) | age < 0 | age > 110)
```

Ages run from `r min(ages$age, na.rm = TRUE)` to `r max(ages$age, na.rm = TRUE)`,
and none is empty, unreadable or outside 0 to 110. On your tables, **look for**
`NA` or empty values in columns that should always be filled, such as `pid`,
`tran_id`, `dateadm` and `pdx`, and ages your question does not allow.

**What to do.** Decide what an empty value means in each column: unknown, not
applicable or an error. Then write filters that say so: `filter(x != "")` drops
empty text and `NA` alike, while `filter(!is.na(x))` keeps empty text. Choose
the plausible range of ages from your question (0 is a real age for a newborn),
and count the records outside it in your flow chart rather than dropping them
unseen.

## A checklist before analysis

Run these on the tables you will use, and keep what they find:

- **Dates:** audit every date you use, by table, read the raw text of the
  failures, and count stays that end before they start.
- **Months:** count records by table and month, and explain any gap, jump or
  overlap.
- **Keys:** check that no `tran_id` repeats, and look at anyone with two records
  on one day.
- **People across tables:** windows across tables assume `pid` means the same
  person in every table you stack; confirm this for your tables.
- **Length of stay:** compare `los`, and columns like it, with the dates, and
  choose which to use.
- **Codes:** check the shape of the codes in every column you search, and clean
  them before your own comparisons.
- **Empty values and ranges:** count `NA` and `""` in the columns you rely on,
  and check ages for impossible values.
- **Decisions:** write down what each check found and what you decided, with
  counts, for your methods.

Next: [Using THIP data responsibly](responsible-use.html) sets out what THIP's
conditions ask of you, and what you may take out of THIP.

```{r disconnect, include = FALSE}
DBI::dbDisconnect(con)
```
